title: Paul Blart: Mall Cop
full_review:
Chivalry is not dead. At least not inside New Jersey's West Orange Pavilion Mall.

The lovably hapless hero of the largely good-natured slapstick comedy "Paul Blart: Mall Cop" (Columbia) embodies many other qualities infrequently championed on-screen nowadays. They include honesty, diligence and respect. And because he exhibits genuine concern for those, like himself, who don't fit the ideal body mold in our looks-conscious society, the pratfall-stuffed "Blart" overcomes a few moderately untoward moments, mostly attributable to sexual innuendo, and affirms a positive message.

Kevin James' flair for physical humor and appetite for self-deprecation carry the project. In addition to co-writing the screenplay, he stars as the titular plus-size security guard who valiantly defends his workplace from a pack of acrobatic thieves on the busiest shopping day of the year.

Having sworn a private oath to protect everyone who steps foot inside this suburban retail mecca, Paul takes his job much more seriously than shoppers take him, or than his colleagues take their duties. He patrols on a Segway, acting officiously yet with everyone's safety uppermost in mind.

His chief flaw is hypoglycemia, which is really just an excuse for using food to self-medicate -- or, as he puts it, "fill the cracks of the heart." Paul's body shows the effects of his habit of ingesting sugar whenever he's tense; and he's constantly battling the assumption he's a loser because he's heavy.

Depressed after failing the physical fitness portion of the state police exam for the eighth time, Paul is consoled at the outset by his mother (Shirley Knight) and a slab of pie smeared with peanut butter. We learn that his wife was an illegal alien who married him to secure citizenship and then took off, leaving him to raise their daughter, Maya (Raini Rodriguez). She and her grandmother want Paul to be happy and urge him to find a girlfriend. They even register him on an Internet dating site.

But he has a crush on Amy (Jayma Mays), a new employee who sells hair extensions at one of the mall's kiosks, "Unbeweaveable." Paul's fumbling attempts to court her are sunk during a night out with other mall workers when he gets embarrassingly inebriated.

His chance to prove his worthiness comes a few days later, on Black Friday, the busiest shopping day of the year. A gang with extreme-sports skills -- portrayed by actual skateboarders, bikers and athletes from the X-Games -- overruns the mall and takes hostages. Their quarry is $30 million worth of credit-card information.

Although "Paul Blart: Mall Cop" never stops making fun of its protagonist and, by implication, all those of ample girth, it's not especially mean or vulgar. Director Steve Carr's effort is not riotously funny or a sterling piece of craftsmanship either, but its faults can be overlooked given this salubrious lesson: Accept who you are, while always trying to improve yourself. A good tagline for the movie would be a request Paul makes of Amy midway through, "Don't write me off."

The film contains frequent violence of a slapstick nature, some suggestive humor, several instances of crude and crass language, and one sequence involving alcohol use. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.
